This vignette will showcase all of the basic functionality found in the `varkit` package.

## Setup

We start off by loading the package and defining the path to the VCF file we
wish to load. The file can be either compressed or uncompressed, but for this
example we will use a block-gzipped VCF:

```{r setup}
library(varkit)

# Normally you would define a path like this:
path <- "path/to/your/file.vcf.gz"

# But we will use example data included with the package here
path <- system.file("extdata", "celegans.vcf.gz", package = "varkit")
```

## Loading a VCF into R

In its simplest form you would load a VCF file into memory like so:

```{r read_simple, eval = FALSE}
vcf <- read_vcf(path)
```

However, it is good practice to first validate if the VCF header is parsed correctly:

```{r header}
header <- read_vcf_header(path)
print(header)
```

> NOTE: Many VarKit functions return a 'tibble', which can be treated as a regular
> `data.frame`, but it displays more compactly when printed to the console.

The most important information here is the column names, which are printed last
(located under `header$col_names`). If the VCF file is recognised correctly it
should list all of the fixed fields and samples present in your VCF. The column
names listed in the header can be provided to the the `col_select` argument of
`read_vcf()` in order to exclude them (the syntax is identical to
`readr::read_table`). This is useful if you want to exclude specific samples, or
if you know you are not going to use certain fixed fields and want to save
memory.

For example here we exclude the "INFO" and "FILTER" fixed fields and the sample "N2":

```{r read}
vcf <- read_vcf(path, col_select = c(-info, -filter, -N2))
print(vcf)
```

## Accessing specific fields

The `read_vcf()` function returns a special "varkit" object that holds all of
the information parsed from the VCF. This information should be accessed through
designated functions, the most important of which are:

```{r access}
samples(vcf)

site(vcf)

geno(vcf)
```

> This syntax is similar to for example accessing the column names of a data
> frame `colnames(df)`.

## Getting help

Functions like `read_vcf()` and `read_vcf_header()` return objects with special
classes, giving them access to an array of build-in functions. To check which
functions are available for any given object use the `vakit_help()` function:

```{r help}
varkit_help(vcf)
```

## Accessing header metadata

In this example, the header metadata can be accessed both from the `vcf` and
`header` objects, like so:

```{r metdata}
meta(vcf) # OR meta(header)
```

However, you might notice that although the returned object is a data frame,
most of the information stored in the `$value` column and cannot be easily
accessed. VarKit provides a function to parse these values, but this requires
you to select the type of field that should be parsed. You can get an overview
of the available field types using:

```{r meta_summary}
parse_meta(vcf)
```

Using this information we can then provide the `parse_meta()` function the
desired type we want to extract. For example we can lookup what the different
values in the INFO fields mean, or we can access the size of the contigs:

```{r meta_parse}
parse_meta(vcf, "INFO")

parse_meta(vcf, "contig")
```

## Masking

A common operation when working with VCF is excluding specific sites based on
various criteria. In VarKit this is achieved through the `mask()` function,
which requires you to input a logical vector (TRUE if the site should be
masked). For this example we will mask/hide all sites on chromosome I:

```{r mask}
# This is a logical vector
mask_site <- site(vcf, "chrom") == "I"

# Be sure to reassign the returned object to `vcf` otherwise the mask will not take effect
vcf <- mask(vcf, mask_site)

# Use the summary function to check the number of visible sites
summary(vcf)$indices
```

Now if we fetch data from the VCF object the masked sites will no longer be
returned. For example if we retrieve the site information (fixed fields) we can
see that the sites with CHROM = "I" are missing (if you look back, you can see
that they were previously on top):

```{r mask_check}
site(vcf)
```

It is important to note that masking can be performed multiple times in
sequence, which will cause sites in **either** mask to be excluded. To
demonstrate this we will only mask sites matching to an external data frame on
the 'chrom', 'pos', and 'alt' columns using the `has_join()` function.

```{r mask_seq}
# Let's use a data frame this time around
sites_to_mask <- dplyr::filter(site(vcf), qual < 3000)
nrow(sites_to_mask)

vcf <- mask(vcf, has_join(site, sites_to_mask, by = c("chrom", "pos", "alt")))
summary(vcf)$indices
```

You can see that this filter masked an additional 3 sites.

### Masking sites without variation

A common task after subsetting or converting VCF files is removing/masking sites
that no longer contain variation. Here we limit the function to only looking
within the GT field (similar to using `parse_geno()`), but the second argument
is optional:

```{r mask_variation}
# Only look at the GT field, obtained by parse_geno(vcf, type = "GT")
vcf <- mask_sites_without_variation(vcf, parse_geno_type = "GT")
summary(vcf)$indices
```

If you compare with the previous `summary()` you can see that 1 additional site was
masked because it lacked variation.

### Using multiple masks

This process is called 'masking' not 'removing' sites, because the sites are not
actually removed from memory, they are just skipped by the VarKit functions.
This allows you to quickly unmask sites or restore an exported set of masked sites.

In this example we will fist export the mask we just created (which masks sites
on CHROM = "I" or sites with a QUAL < 3000) and assign it to the `my_mask`
variable, then we will remove the mask from the vcf object which verify through
the `summary()` function:

```{r mask_export}
my_mask <- export_mask(vcf)
vcf <- unmask_all(vcf)
summary(vcf)$indices
```

Then if we later decide that we need the mask again, we can import it:

```{r mask_import}
vcf <- import_mask(vcf, my_mask)
summary(vcf)$indices
```

In this way you could use different masks for different parts of your
analysis/script.

### Removing sites

In some cases, e.g. when you need to free memory or when you need maximum lookup
speed, it is possible to entirely remove sites from memory (meaning they cannot
be retrieved by unmasking):

```{r mask_remove}
reduced_vcf <- delete_masked_sites(vcf)
summary(reduced_vcf)$indices
```

## Writing VCF files

Varkit also has the ability to write VCF files. This is useful for example when
you have removed specific sites or samples and want to write the reduced file.

Moreover, masks are also stored in the FILTER column of the resulting VCF file
if `replace_filter = TRUE`, allowing you to save and load a masked VCF:

```{r save_masked_vcf}
temp_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".vcf")
write_vcf(vcf, file = temp_file, replace_filter = TRUE)

read_vcf(temp_file)
```

> NOTE: R does not support writing in the block-gzipped format (only the regular
> gzip format) that is expected by many other tools. To achieve this you can
> export to plain ".vcf" and convert the file using the "bgzip" CLI (and "tabix"
> for indexing).

## Detecting linkage between sites

Lastly, the VarKit package provides functionality to detect and remove linkage
between sites. Internally this package reimplements `stats::cor(..., method =
"pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")` to utilize BLAS, thus using a faster
BLAS library like openBLAS should improve performance.

In order for this to work `geno(vcf)` should contain only **numeric** values (or
NA). Most likely your genotype fields will be in the string format and thus need
to be converted. How to achieve this is highly circumstantial and will require
manual parsing/conversion. For tips take a look at the "Notes for advanced
users" section at the bottom.

As you might have noticed, the example file contains complex genotypes that
consist of multiple parts (delimited by a colon) that are described in the
'format' column of `site(vcf)`. We first extract the genotype calls (GT, e.g.
"0/1") from these complex fields, which we then convert to numeric dosages using
a hidden function:

```{r convert_geno}
# Overwriting geno(vcf) is only allowed when it has no masked sites
vcf <- unmask_all(vcf)
geno(vcf) <- parse_geno(vcf, type = "GT")
# The function below is not exported as it is not very robust, use it with caution!
geno(vcf) <- varkit:::.bi_gt2dosage(geno(vcf))
```

Now we run `find_linked_sites()` to obtain a list of dataframes with sites that
have an R^2^ above the specified cutoff for each CHROM. Then we call
`resolve_links()` to determine which sites should be excluded if we want to
remove as many of the detected links as possible (very few links could remain).

```{r linked_sites, results = 'hide'}
links <- find_linked_sites(vcf, cutoff = 0.9, size_bp = 1e5, windows = 2, by_chrom = TRUE, cores = 1)
lgraph <- resolve_links(links, cores = 1)
```

> Here we use a sliding window spanning 2 (`n_window`) X 1e5 base pairs
> (`window_bp_size`) = 2e5 bases to the left AND right (effectively 4e5 bases)
> of any given site. You could use any combination of `n_window` and
> `window_size_bp` to achieve this number, but there is a trade-off in
> computational efficientcy that you should try to balance. Generally one should
> first increase `window_size_bp` to 1e5 and then achieve a higher size by
> increasing `n_window` above 1. The `n_window` argument can also be set to a
> negative number, in which case all sites within each CHROM are compared (the
> window size will still impact performance). To enable comparisons between
> chromosomes set `by_chrom` to FALSE (when `n_window > 0` only chromosomes that
> follow one another in the VCF are compared).

```{r linked_sites_summary}
summary(lgraph, vcf = vcf)
```

This will return a directed acyclic graph in which each node is labeled with the
(column) index of a site in the **unmasked** vcf. Each node that should be
removed to reduce linkage is connected to a note that will be retained and is
guaranteed to have an R^2^ above the cutoff (retained -> removed). Please refer
to the Igraph package for information on working with these graphs.

Luckily there is no need to understand graph theory as the removal of linked
sites can be automated by passing the graph as the second argument to the
`mask()` function. In the resulting vcf, for each group of linked sites, the
single best site is retained and all others are masked, thus representing the
most amount of information with the least amount of variants.

```{r mask_linked}
vcf <- mask(vcf, site = is_linked(lgraph, vcf = .))
summary(vcf)$indices
```
